title: Governance, Safety & Risk Management
intro: This domain tests whether you can make Claude-based systems safe to operate in the real world: enforcing hard rules with the right kinds of controls, anticipating how LLM systems fail, placing humans where their judgment actually matters, satisfying regulators through deployment architecture, and treating fairness and transparency as engineering requirements. Exam questions are scenario-based: you will be given a company, a design, and a constraint, and asked to pick the response that reflects sound risk reasoning rather than the one that merely sounds cautious.

objectives.explanation:
Guardrails are the mechanisms that keep an LLM system inside its intended envelope of behavior. The essential mental model is layered defense: system-prompt instructions shape behavior, input filters screen what reaches the model, output validation (classifiers, parsers, rules) checks what leaves it, tool permission scoping limits what an agent can actually do, and rate limits bound how fast damage can accumulate. No single layer is reliable on its own, and the layers differ in kind, not just position.

The most important distinction on the exam is between probabilistic and deterministic controls. Anything enforced by asking the model — system-prompt rules, refusal instructions, 'never do X' clauses — is probabilistic: it lowers the rate of violations but cannot drive it to zero, and adversarial pressure (jailbreaks, prompt injection) raises the failure rate. Anything enforced outside the model — an API that rejects over-limit requests, a read-only database role, a parser that blocks non-SELECT statements, a classifier gate before publication — is deterministic with respect to the model: the model cannot talk its way past it. Hard requirements (regulatory rules, financial limits, destructive-action bans) must rest on deterministic layers; instructions are hygiene, not enforcement.

Two further design decisions recur. First, blocking versus flagging: when an output or action is public, irreversible, or high-harm, fail closed — block on detection and route to review before release. When errors are cheap and recoverable, flag and review asynchronously to preserve throughput. Second, design assuming bypass: jailbreak and injection resistance is inherently probabilistic, so the safety case for a system rests on bounding the impact of a successful bypass — least-privilege tools, scoped credentials, validated outputs, monitoring — not on claiming any layer is unbreakable.
objectives.whyItMatters: In production, the difference between an embarrassing transcript and a regulatory incident or financial loss is usually whether a hard rule was enforced in the prompt or in the architecture. Teams routinely ship instruction-only controls because they are fast to write, then discover under adversarial traffic that a percentage failure rate on thousands of daily interactions is a steady stream of real violations. Architects are the people expected to catch this before launch.

examples.title: Refund agent with a policy cap
examples.body: A support agent can issue refunds, and policy caps agent-initiated refunds at $200. The first design states the cap in the system prompt; a red-team exercise talks the agent into a $5,000 refund via injected instructions in a forwarded email. The fix is layered: the refunds API itself rejects any agent request above $200 (deterministic enforcement the model cannot override), requests above the threshold pause for manager approval (human gate on the policy-defined boundary), and the prompt instruction stays as a first-line behavioral nudge. After the fix, a fully compromised agent can still only do what the API permits — the blast radius, not the persuasion, is what changed.

examples.title: Choosing block vs flag for a public content pipeline
examples.body: A retailer auto-publishes thousands of AI-generated product answers daily, with a safety classifier flagging about 4% of drafts, half of them false positives. Publishing flagged drafts and reviewing next day means harmful content reaches customers before any human sees it. The right call is to fail closed: flagged drafts are held, reviewed, then published. The cost is a short delay on some correct answers; the benefit is that every true positive is prevented rather than recalled. The decision follows from the output being public and hard to recall, not from the classifier's precision.

pitfalls: Treating a hardened system prompt as enforcement for a hard requirement — instructions reduce violation frequency but cannot guarantee zero, so regulatory and financial rules need deterministic backstops.
Promising or demanding a 'jailbreak-proof' system — resistance is probabilistic over an open-ended input space, so mature designs bound the impact of bypass instead of claiming it cannot happen.
Relying on detective controls (logs, dashboards, weekly audits) for irreversible actions — detection after money moves or content publishes is incident response, not a guardrail.
Regenerating outputs until they pass your own safety classifier — this optimizes against the guardrail and ships subtler versions of the same problem with no human judgment applied.
Confusing a human confirmation click with a control when the confirmer cannot evaluate what they are approving, such as analysts approving SQL they cannot read.

objectives.objective: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
objectives.explanation:
LLM systems fail in characteristic ways, and the exam expects you to recognize each mode from its symptoms and name the right architectural response. Hallucination: the model generates plausible text, not verified fact, and expresses no less confidence when fabricating — so fluency is never evidence, and verification (grounding in retrieved sources, checking citations against ground truth) must live outside the model. Prompt injection comes in two forms: direct (the user attacks) and indirect (instructions hidden in content the model reads — retrieved documents, web pages, emails, tool results). Indirect injection is the defining new attack surface of agents, because every content source the model reads is an input channel an attacker can write to, and tool access converts injected text into real-world actions.

Several failure modes are properties of the system around the model rather than the model itself. Data leakage often happens through secondary paths: full-prompt logging copies sensitive data into observability systems with weaker access controls and longer retention than the system of record. Automation bias is the erosion of human vigilance as a mostly-right system trains its reviewers to stop checking — visible as rising approval rates, falling review times, and errors surviving review. Cascading failure afflicts chained pipelines: per-step accuracies multiply (three 95% steps yield roughly 86% end to end), and downstream steps confidently build on corrupted upstream output rather than flagging it, so decomposed pipelines need validation between stages.

Finally, non-determinism and model drift are lifecycle risks. The same prompt can yield different outputs across runs, and behavior is not portable across model versions: prompts tuned against one version can regress on the next despite better public benchmarks. Treat a model version change like a major dependency upgrade — gated by regression evaluation on your own golden dataset with a staged rollout. Excessive agency — granting an agent more tools, autonomy, or scope than its task requires — is the multiplier that turns all the above from quality issues into incidents.
objectives.whyItMatters: Risk identification is what separates an architect from an implementer: most LLM incidents in production trace to a known failure mode that nobody named during design review. A team that can say 'this is indirect injection reaching a privileged tool' or 'this is automation bias hollowing out our review layer' can fix the cause; a team that cannot will patch symptoms indefinitely while the exposure persists.

examples.title: Diagnosing the radiology review failure
examples.body: A tool drafts findings summaries for radiologist review. Six months in, agreement runs 98%, review time has collapsed, and missed findings trace to uncorrected draft errors. The tempting diagnoses — model drift, hallucination — describe how errors entered the drafts, but the audit's real finding is that the human layer meant to catch them stopped functioning. That is automation bias, and the fix is procedural: blind second reads on a sample, requiring reviewers to record key findings before seeing the draft, and tracking correction rates as a health metric for the review layer itself. Naming the failure mode correctly changes what you fix.

examples.title: The chained-pipeline launch argument
examples.body: A contract-intake pipeline has three Claude stages, each 95% accurate in isolation, and the team calls it launch-ready. Multiplying through gives roughly 86% end to end, and the practical number is worse because an extraction error is silently laundered through the comparison and drafting stages into a polished, wrong memo. The architectural answer is inter-stage validation: schema checks on extracted terms, confidence gates that route uncertain extractions to review, and sampled end-to-end audits — catching errors where they enter rather than shipping them with a professional finish.

pitfalls: Assuming a fluent, confident answer is more likely to be true — models signal no uncertainty when hallucinating, so confidence calibration must come from external verification, not tone.
Threat-modeling only the user as attacker — indirect injection arrives through retrieved documents, web content, and tool results, so any third-party content source is part of the attack surface.
Forgetting that logs, analytics copies, and caches are data stores — prompt logging can recreate the exact exposure your access controls were built to prevent.
Extrapolating per-component accuracy to system accuracy in chained pipelines — errors compound and hide, so end-to-end evaluation and inter-stage checks are mandatory.
Swapping model versions on benchmark strength alone — behavior tuned against one version does not transfer, so migrations need your own regression suite and a staged rollout.

objectives.explanation:
Human-in-the-loop design is fundamentally an allocation problem: human attention is scarce and expensive, so it must be spent where it changes outcomes. The controlling variables are impact and reversibility. Actions that are high-impact and irreversible — wire transfers, account freezes, medical escalations, benefit denials — get mandatory pre-action approval gates: the action pauses until a human decides. Outputs that are recoverable — drafts, summaries, internal notes — get review woven into the natural workflow (an officer edits before sending) or sampled review sized to detect systemic regressions rather than to inspect every unit.

Routing is the second design lever. Rather than a fixed rule, mature systems use confidence-based and risk-based routing: conversations or cases reach humans when model confidence is low, stakes are high (account value, action type), sentiment signals distress, or automated resolution has repeatedly failed. This concentrates human judgment exactly where the model is least trustworthy, and the thresholds are tunable from outcome data. Escalation should never depend on the affected person diagnosing the failure themselves.

The third pillar is verifying that the human step is real. Mandated review decays into rubber-stamping under volume and habituation — the signatures are near-total approval rates, collapsing review times, and errors surviving review. Countermeasures include seeding known-error cases and measuring catch rates, tracking correction and disagreement rates as health metrics, and reducing review volume so remaining reviews get genuine attention. For consequential decisions about individuals — lending, hiring, benefits — the human must hold actual decision authority, especially on adverse outcomes; a human who merely monitors machine decisions is not meaningful control.
objectives.whyItMatters: HITL is the control regulators, ethics boards, and executives most often ask for, and the one most often implemented as theater. A production system whose 'human review' approves 99.7% of items in 20 seconds each has an audit trail and no safety. Architects who can place gates by reversibility, route by confidence, and instrument the review layer itself deliver oversight that actually functions when the model is wrong.

examples.title: Allocating oversight in a treasury agent
examples.body: An agent drafts client emails, prepares research notes, and initiates wire transfers. Uniform review of all three wastes scarce attention and breeds fatigue; reviewing only by 'external consequences' groups recoverable emails with unrecoverable wires. The defensible allocation follows reversibility: wires get a mandatory pre-execution approval gate because settlement cannot be undone; emails and notes ship through lightweight or sampled review because errors are correctable in the normal course of business. Friction lands only where the risk justifies it.

examples.title: Detecting the rubber stamp
examples.body: An insurer requires nurse review of every AI-drafted prior-authorization recommendation. Metrics show 300 reviews per nurse per day, 99.7% approval, 20-second average review. Leadership reads this as model quality; the architect should read it as an unverifiable control. The fix is to make review quality observable — seed drafts with known errors and measure the catch rate, track correction rates over time — and to shrink volume via confidence routing so nurses see only cases where their judgment is genuinely needed. A control you cannot verify is working must be assumed broken.

pitfalls: Applying one uniform review policy to all outputs — uniformity dilutes attention across low-risk items and degrades vigilance on the actions that genuinely need it.
Using retrospective review (digests, weekly audits) for immediate-impact actions — by the time a mishandled account freeze or transfer is spotted, the harm has landed.
Assuming a mandated human step works because it exists — without catch-rate or disagreement instrumentation, rubber-stamping is invisible until an incident exposes it.
Making escalation depend on the user asking for a human — the people most harmed by model failure are often the least able to recognize it.
Letting the model auto-finalize 'clear-cut' consequential decisions — the confidence rating is itself a model output and can be systematically wrong for subgroups.

objectives.objective: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
objectives.explanation:
The unifying idea for this objective is that compliance is a property of the deployment architecture, not of the model. The same Claude model can be fully compliant or flatly non-compliant depending on what data reaches it, through which environment, under which contracts, and with what retention. Exam scenarios test whether you reach for the architectural and contractual mechanism rather than a generic security measure or a paperwork gesture.

GDPR governs personal data of people in the EU. The load-bearing concepts are: a lawful basis for processing; data minimization (send the model only the fields the purpose requires — shipping a full CRM record for a shipping question over-processes by design); the right to erasure, which applies to every copy of the data, including prompts persisted in logs, analytics warehouses, and caches, so deletion propagation must be designed in; data residency and lawful transfer mechanisms for processing outside the EU; and the controller–processor structure — the model provider acts as a processor or sub-processor under a data processing agreement, disclosed in the chain so customer obligations flow down every hop. Pseudonymized data is still personal data.

HIPAA governs protected health information held by covered entities and their business associates. Sending PHI to a model provider requires a signed Business Associate Agreement with that provider — encryption and security certifications are necessary but do not substitute — plus minimum-necessary data flows and PHI-aware handling in every component that touches it, including logs. FedRAMP is the US federal authorization program for cloud services: agencies consume cloud AI only through FedRAMP-authorized environments (for example, Claude offered via an authorized cloud platform), and no commercial security posture or private contract substitutes for authorization. Across all three regimes, features like zero-data-retention modes, regional processing, audit trails, and documented log retention are the concrete levers architects configure.
objectives.whyItMatters: Compliance failures are among the few LLM risks that convert directly into fines, lost contracts, and blocked launches: an enterprise deal stalls on a missing DPA disclosure, a healthcare integration is illegal without a BAA regardless of its security quality, and a federal proposal is disqualified outright if the deployment path is not authorized. Architects are expected to know which instrument each regime demands before a single record flows.

examples.title: The 'HIPAA-ready because encrypted' fallacy
examples.body: A telehealth CTO argues that encrypted API traffic makes a Claude intake-summarization feature HIPAA-ready. The architect must insist on the actual preconditions: a signed BAA with the model provider before any PHI flows, retention configuration reviewed, access to prompts and logs scoped, and every component in the path — including observability tooling — treated as PHI-bearing. De-identification sounds like an escape hatch, but reliably stripping all identifiers from conversational clinical text is fragile, and the summaries must map back to patients anyway. The BAA-backed architecture is the robust posture.

examples.title: Erasure request meets the shadow copies
examples.body: A European neobank receives a right-to-erasure request and discovers the customer's chat transcripts persist in an analytics warehouse and a debug log store long after the CRM profile is deleted. The lesson is data lineage: personal data must be tracked into every system it propagates to, and erasure implemented as a coordinated capability across all copies — designed before launch, not improvised per request. Retention limits and crypto-shredding can be components of the answer, but neither replaces knowing where the data went and being able to delete it there.

pitfalls: Treating encryption, SOC 2, or ISO certifications as regulatory compliance — they are security evidence, not the legal instruments (BAA, DPA, FedRAMP authorization) each regime actually requires.
Sending maximal context 'for better answers' in regulated deployments — data minimization is an architectural obligation, and over-broad prompts are over-processing by design.
Claiming pseudonymization takes data out of GDPR scope — if the organization can re-link tokens to people, it remains personal data with full obligations attached.
Forgetting that prompts and completions persisted in logs, analytics, and caches are copies subject to erasure, retention, and access rules just like the primary store.
Proposing commercial API endpoints for US federal workloads — agencies require FedRAMP-authorized deployment environments, and no privately negotiated terms substitute.

objectives.objective: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
objectives.explanation:
Ethical AI on this exam is tested as engineering discipline, not philosophy. Bias enters through training data and through the populations and prompts a system meets in production, and it is invisible in aggregate metrics: a model can match human judgments 94% overall while systematically disadvantaging one group. The response is measurement — disparate-impact testing that compares score distributions and selection rates across demographic groups on representative data, performed before launch and continuously afterward. Blinding inputs (removing names and demographics) does not achieve fairness, because proxy features — zip codes, school names, career gaps, writing style — carry the same signal, and blinding also makes disparity harder to measure. Fairness findings are perishable: population shift, prompt revisions, and model upgrades each invalidate the baseline, so mature systems treat fairness like a production SLO with change-triggered re-assessment.

Transparency means affected people know that AI participates in decisions and communications that matter to them, and can understand the principal factors behind outcomes that affect them. Disclosure obligations grow with the sensitivity of the relationship — patients, applicants, benefit claimants — and concealment discovered later costs far more trust than honest framing would have. Contestability completes the pillar: a person affected by an AI-influenced decision needs a route to see why, and to trigger re-evaluation by a human with authority to change the outcome. Appeals are not just individual justice; they are the institution's best sensor for systematic error.

The hardest ethical line is around consequential decisions — lending, hiring, housing, benefits. Fully automating adverse decisions in these domains is the pattern to refuse: the architecture should keep humans as the decision-makers (at minimum on denials), backed by fairness testing and appeal paths. High agreement with historical human decisions is not a defense, since faithful reproduction of biased history is itself the harm to prevent.
objectives.whyItMatters: Ethical failures compound differently from technical ones: a biased screening system can silently harm thousands of people before any metric flags it, and the discovery — often by journalists or regulators rather than the team — brings legal exposure, mandated shutdowns, and durable reputational damage. Jurisdictions are also codifying these expectations into law, so contestability, disclosure, and impact testing are increasingly requirements, not aspirations.

examples.title: The lender that wanted full automation
examples.body: A consumer lender proposes letting Claude output approve/decline decisions directly to applicants, citing 94% agreement with human underwriters. The architect's job is to reframe: agreement with historical decisions can reproduce historical bias, credit is a consequential determination about individuals, and the required package is structural — the model recommends, human underwriters decide (especially declines), disparate-impact testing runs across protected groups before and after launch, and applicants get an appeal path. Explanations attached to automated declines improve transparency but do not substitute for human authority and measured fairness.

examples.title: Fairness after nine months of drift
examples.body: A marketplace screening system passed disparate-impact assessment at launch; since then the applicant pool shifted regionally, the prompt changed twice, and the model was upgraded once. The pre-launch certificate no longer describes the running system: fairness is a property of a specific configuration meeting a specific population, and all of it changed. The correct posture is continuous outcome monitoring by group with re-assessment triggered by material change — and a warning that stable aggregate approval rates prove nothing, since offsetting subgroup shifts hide inside flat averages.

pitfalls: Equating input blindness with fairness — removing demographic fields leaves proxy features intact and makes disparate impact harder to measure, not less likely to occur.
Trusting aggregate accuracy or stable overall rates — subgroup harms hide inside averages, which is exactly why measurement must be disaggregated by group.
Treating fairness assessment as a one-time launch gate — population shift, prompt edits, and model upgrades each invalidate the baseline and should trigger re-assessment.
Offering explanations or model cards as a substitute for contestability — documentation informs, but affected individuals need a human appeal that can actually change the outcome.
Validating a consequential-decision system by agreement with historical human decisions — if the history was biased, high concordance measures faithful reproduction of the bias.
